title: Those Who Rise in Rank Bear No Grudge
intro: A Beirut printing of Antarah’s Diwan gives this poem to the warrior of Abs and sets it in a challenge to al-Nu'man. The man once sent to tend camels now defends their owners and claims his black skin as a lineage of his own. The poem is absent from the rhyme index of Muhammad Sa'id Mawlawi’s edition, based on six manuscripts. Mishil Salim Kumayd also pointed out in Lughat al-Arab how closely the last verse echoes al-Mutanabbi. The attribution remains uncertain.

translation: Those who rise in rank bear no grudge.
A quick temper never wins high standing.
1.sharh: The first half looks at people already held in honour and the second at those who aspire to it. It is a striking rule of restraint for a speaker about to issue a challenge.

translation: A man enslaved to a people cannot oppose them
when they slight him. He courts their favour when they blame him.
2.sharh: He describes an unequal bargain. His masters may give offence, yet it falls to the enslaved man to conciliate them when they in turn complain.

translation: Once I tended their camels.
Today I guard their lands whenever disaster strikes.
3.sharh: The same men who once assigned him the herd now depend on him for the safety of the whole pasture. The change in scale measures his changed place among them.

translation: God bless the sons of Abs. They have sired
as noble men as any Arab people has borne.
4.sharh: He praises Abs for the people it breeds. Since he has just identified himself as its defender, the compliment also lays a claim to membership.

translation: If they shame me for my black skin, it is my lineage
in battle, when lineage fails me.
5.sharh: Lineage is repeated with a changed meaning. The colour others use to exclude him makes the man who fought for them unmistakable.

translation: If you think, Nu'man, that my hand
cannot reach you, the days turn.
6.sharh: A short hand is a limit on a man’s power to reach another. The threat allows the king his present advantage and quietly gives it an expiry date.

translation: Today, Nu'man, you will learn what manner of man
your brother meets, so sure of his bands of men.
7.sharh: He holds back the description of the fighter. First comes the prince’s brother, whose confidence has been inflated by the number of men at his back.

translation: Snakes may feel soft to the touch.
When they turn, destruction lies in their fangs.
8.sharh: The danger is disclosed by a movement. The very hand that registered only softness may be within reach of the fangs when the snake turns.

translation: A man who wades smiling into the thick of battle
comes back with his spearhead dyed.
9.sharh: The young man promised two verses earlier now has a smile on his face. The colour on his spearpoint supplies the other side of that picture.

translation: When he draws his blade, its striking edges run,
the air lights up and its veils split open.
10.sharh: The flowing edge suggests blood, the sudden light the flash of steel. In Arabic the verb for drawing the blade almost runs into the sound of the verb for flowing.

translation: The horses bear witness that I hold them in check
while the thrusting flares like sparks of fire.
11.sharh: The horses themselves can testify to the hand on the reins. Amid an exchange of thrusts like flying sparks, checking their rush is as much a feat as charging.

translation: When I meet enemies on a field of battle,
I leave their overconfident host to be plundered.
12.sharh: The host begins as a body confident of its strength and ends as plunder at other people’s disposal. The passive verb leaves open who takes what.

translation: Mine are the lives, the flesh belongs to the birds,
the bones to the beasts, the spoils to the horsemen.
13.sharh: The verse is a distribution of spoils extending beyond the human victors. The speaker reserves the taking of lives, a more chilling claim than a share of the equipment.

translation: May God keep those noblemen in my sight,
human on foot, jinn when mounted.
14.sharh: Dismounted, the riders are men one could meet. In the saddle they acquire the extraordinary speed and powers associated with jinn.

translation: Lions of the thicket, yet their only fangs
are spearpoints and keen Indian swords.
15.sharh: The description carries the lion comparison through to its teeth. Spears and swords supply what the mounted men’s human mouths lack.

translation: Lean horses of A'waj’s stock carry them along,
wolf-like, with the fine taper of their necks.
16.sharh: The riders’ mounts have been conditioned for speed. Their lean outlines bring wolves to mind, following the lions the riders have just been called.

translation: I keep facing the horses’ breasts, pouring forward
with thrusts till saddle and breast strap cry out.
17.sharh: Horses’ chests tell us he meets a charge head-on. Strain makes even the tack seem to find a voice.

translation: If the blind had me within their eyelids, they would see.
If the mute had me in their mouths, they would speak.
18.sharh: He imagines his presence restoring sight and speech. The Arabic leaves the thing present in eye or mouth unnamed, as though his person and his fame were interchangeable.

translation: The dust on the day the horsemen give chase bears me witness,
as do blows, thrusts, pens and books.
19.sharh: Dust and weapons can testify to what happened in the field. Pens and books carry that testimony elsewhere, in a catalogue especially close to the famous boast of al-Mutanabbi.

1.1.3.head: حِقد
1.1.3.meaning: A grudge deliberately nursed after an injury.

1.1.7.head: رُتبَة
1.1.7.meaning: A rank of honour or authority.

2.1.3-4.head: عَبد قَوم
2.1.3-4.meaning: “A people’s slave”, a man subject to their power.

2.2.3.head: اِستَرضى
2.2.3.meaning: Sought to conciliate an offended person.

3.2.3.head: حِمى
3.2.3.meaning: A protected territory, especially a reserved pasture.

4.1.1-2.head: لِلَّهِ دَرُّهُ
4.1.1-2.meaning: “To God belongs their yield”, a formula of admiration.

4.1.3-4.head: بَنو عَبس
4.1.3-4.meaning: Banu Abs, the tribe to which the heroic tradition attaches Antarah.

5.2.2.head: نِزال
5.2.2.meaning: An encounter with an opponent at close quarters.

5.2.6.head: نَسَب
5.2.6.meaning: Descent by a recognised line of ancestors.

6.1.5.head: النُّعمان
6.1.5.meaning: Al-Nu'man ibn al-Mundhir, king of al-Hira according to the printed heading.

6.2.1-2.head: قَصيرَة عَنكَ
6.2.1-2.meaning: “Short of reaching you”, beyond the reach of my power.

7.1.5-6.head: أَيّ فَتى
7.1.5-6.meaning: “What a young man”, a challenge to discover his calibre.

7.2.6.head: عُصبَة
7.2.6.meaning: Bands of men bound together for support.

8.1.5.head: مَلمَس
8.1.5.meaning: The surface as it feels to the hand.

9.1.3.head: غِمار
9.1.3.meaning: The engulfing depths, here the thick of battle. The Beirut Diwan and Jawahir al-adab have “the dust of battle”. Abd Allah al-Tayyib also gives “the depths”.

9.2.4.head: اِختَضَبَ
9.2.4.meaning: Took a dye, here a coating of blood.

10.1.5.head: مَضرِب
10.1.5.meaning: The part of the sword edge that strikes.

11.1.5.head: كَفكَفَ
11.1.5.meaning: Checked a rush, holding the horses back.

13.2.4.head: سَلَب
13.2.4.meaning: Equipment and clothing taken from a defeated fighter.

14.1.6.head: غِطريف
14.1.6.meaning: A noble chief, here one of the speaker’s companions.

14.2.4.head: جِنّ
14.2.4.meaning: Jinn, beings whose extraordinary powers suggest the riders’ uncanny speed.

15.2.2.head: سِنان
15.2.2.meaning: Spearheads, the fangs of these human lions.

15.2.3-4.head: الهِندِيَّة القُضُب
15.2.3-4.meaning: “Indian cutters”, keen swords associated with India.

16.1.1.head: حَدا
16.1.1.meaning: Urged onward. The Beirut Diwan and Jawahir al-adab give “gallop” here.

16.1.3.head: أَعوَجِيَّة
16.1.3.meaning: A'waji horses, traced to the celebrated stallion A'waj. The verse card prints the plural. The sung vowel leaves the number hard to distinguish.

16.2.2.head: سِرحان
16.2.2.meaning: A wolf, used as a comparison for a lean mount.

17.2.5.head: لَبَب
17.2.5.meaning: A breast strap that holds the saddle in place.
